title: Opinions
tagline: Give an opinion, disagree politely, connect your ideas.
canDo: You can hold your own in a family argument

grammar.title: Agreeing takes se
grammar.body: main aap se ittefaq karta hoon (I agree with you). main is baat se ittefaq nahin karta (I don't agree with this point).

grammar.title: Connectors
grammar.body: halanke (although), balke (but rather: corrects what came before), is ke bawajood (despite that), is liye (so), kyunke (because), misaal ke taur par (for example), ek taraf… doosri taraf… (on one hand… on the other…).

grammar.title: ke: that
grammar.body: baat yeh hai ke… (the thing is that…), mera khayal hai ke… (I think that…), sach to yeh hai ke… (the truth is that…). ke introduces the whole next clause.

lessons.title: Mere khayal mein
lessons.blurb: Have an opinion. Say it out loud. In Urdu.
lessons.canDo: You can give your opinion and agree or disagree politely

teach.tip: Put it at the front of any sentence and it becomes an opinion instead of a fight.
X se ittefaq karna: to agree 'from' X.
Softer than 'you're wrong'. Means exactly the same.

exercises.question: What does Abbu think is Pakistan's weak point?

options.feedback: He says the bowling is achhi. Listen for kamzor.
That's Nani's concern, and it is a serious one.

exercises.setup: Match day. The TV is on. So is everyone's opinion.

exercises.explain: You agree 'from' someone: aap se ittefaq.

lessons.title: Halanke, balke
lessons.blurb: The connectors that make you sound like you've thought about it.
lessons.canDo: You can link ideas with although, rather, despite and so

teach.tip: is liye = so. kyunke = because. Cause and effect, in either order.

exercises.question: What is Ammi's point in favour of Karachi?

options.feedback: A real argument, but not the one she made.

exercises.prompt: “Woh ameer nahin, ___ bohat ameer hai.” (He's not rich, rather he's very rich.)
“Barish thi, ___ hum nahin gaye.” (It was raining, so we didn't go.)

options.feedback: That would mean you went anyway.

lessons.title: Hold your ground
lessons.blurb: Concede a little, push back a lot, then have tea.
lessons.canDo: You can argue a point without starting a feud

teach.tip: Buys you three seconds to work out what the thing actually is.
Concede first, then disagree. It's the lekin that does the work.

exercises.prompt: Nana has made a point. A wrong one. Be diplomatic.

exercises.explain: You want them to hear YOUR point: meri baat.

exercises.prompt: Opening a point, or ending the argument?
End the argument the traditional way.

lessons.title: Mix it up
lessons.blurb: The tea has gone cold. Warm up for the boss.
lessons.canDo: You can use this unit's phrases without a prompt: you can hold your own in a family argument

teach.title: The tea has gone cold
teach.info: That means the argument is a good one. Line up your connectors.

exercises.prompt: Khala is on the phone. Say: “in my opinion”
Nani is waiting. Say: “that's why / so”

boss.title: In Our Day
boss.blurb: Abbu says everything was better in his day. Disagree with him. Respectfully.
boss.scene: Sunday afternoon. Abbu puts down the newspaper, takes off his glasses, and begins a sentence with 'hamare zamane mein'. Everyone else leaves the room.
boss.canDo: You can disagree with an elder, give an example and find the middle ground

options.reaction: 'Gustakhi maaf' first. Smart. He can't even be angry.

b.hint: Aap ki baat theek hai, lekin…

options.reaction: Ammi, from the kitchen: a single loud laugh.

end.title: You won. Sort of
end.text: You disagreed with Abbu, backed it up with an example, and finished on speaking terms. He'll tell his friends you argue 'like a lawyer'. From him, that's praise.
